title: Where does an empty ext4 filesystem’s space go?
answer: On a disk of 1 GiB or more, the default 5% reserve for root takes as much space as all the metadata, or more

checks.question: A new 1 TiB ext4 disk shows 93.3% available. What takes most of the missing 6.7%?
checks.answer: The 5% of blocks mke2fs reserves for root by default: 13,421,772 blocks, 3.0 times the 4,495,258 blocks of metadata. The kernel holds back 4,096 more.

checks.question: Of the 1 TiB disk’s metadata, what is the biggest part?
checks.answer: The inode tables: one 256-byte inode for every 16 KiB of disk, 4,194,304 blocks, 93.3% of the metadata. The journal is 1 GiB, 5.8%.

checks.question: Would formatting the 1 TiB disk with -m 0 free any of the metadata?
checks.answer: No. -m 0 only stops reserving blocks for root; the inode tables, journal and other metadata stay. Users could then write all but the metadata and the kernel’s 4,096 blocks.

steps.title: A new 1 GiB disk: users can write only 88.5% of it
steps.line: Predict: no file is written yet. Where did 118.1 MiB go?
steps.caption: We ran mkfs.ext4 1.47.3 with no options on an empty 1 GiB disk, 262,144 blocks of 4096 bytes, mounted it and asked the kernel’s statfs, which df reads. A user other than root can write 231,922 blocks, which df shows as Avail: 88.5% of the disk. The other 30,222 blocks, 11.5%, are unavailable to this writer before any user files are added. Does unavailable mean already occupied? Predict where they went.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 1 GiB”: 2 slices; “statfs after mkfs.ext4”, 4 labelled values.

steps.title: Answer: 5% is held back for root, 1.0 times all the metadata
steps.line: Predict: what fills the 13,019 blocks of metadata?
steps.caption: On a disk of 1 GiB or more, the default 5% reserve for root takes as much space as all the metadata, or more. Without -m, mke2fs reserves 5% of the blocks for root, 13,107 here, held back for privileged use. Those blocks can still be free: the reserve changes who may fill them, not whether metadata occupies them. The metadata, the filesystem’s own structures, is 13,019 blocks, 5.0%, and once mounted the kernel holds back 4,096 more. Free blocks less both reserves is what ordinary users can write. Lowering the root reserve can change that availability without removing a single metadata block.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 1 GiB”: 4 slices; “Where the blocks go”, 7 labelled values. The answer: Root reserve: 5.0%. New in this step: Metadata: 5.0%; Kernel reserve: 1.6%; “Where the blocks go”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: Inode tables are 31.5% of the metadata
steps.line: One 256-byte inode per 16 KiB of disk: 65,536 inodes.
steps.caption: This pie’s whole is the 13,019 metadata blocks. An inode records one file, so mke2fs sets aside a fixed number up front, by the disk’s size type: one inode per 16 KiB of disk for the default type, 512 MiB to under 4 TiB; per 32 KiB for big, under 16 TiB; and per 64 KiB for huge, above that. 1 GiB, of the default type, gets 65,536 inodes of 256 bytes, in tables set aside now: 4,096 blocks, 1.6% of the disk.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Inode tables”, 6 labelled values. This step: Inode tables: 31.5%.

steps.title: The journal is 32 MiB, 62.9% of the metadata
steps.line: It doubles with disk size from 16 MiB to 1 GiB; here 3.1% of the disk.
steps.caption: mke2fs sizes the journal in steps of disk size, doubling from 16 MiB at 128 MiB to 1 GiB at 128 GiB, and no larger after that. 1 GiB gets 8,192 blocks, 32 MiB: 62.9% of the metadata and 3.1% of the disk.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Journal by disk size”, 7 labelled values. This step: Journal: 62.9%; 1 GiB: From 1 GiB: 32 MiB. New in this step: “Journal by disk size”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: The other 731 blocks: copies, bitmaps and the first files
steps.line: Superblock copies in 5 of 8 groups; two bitmaps in every group.
steps.caption: Group 0, group 1 and groups that are powers of 3, 5 or 7 keep a copy of the superblock and group descriptors: 5 of 8 groups, each with 127 spare descriptor blocks for growing the filesystem. Every group has two bitmaps. The root directory, lost+found, the orphan file and an index block take 70 blocks.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Other metadata”, 7 labelled values. This step: Other metadata: 5.6%. New in this step: “Other metadata”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: At -m 5, users can write 88.5%, 93.3%, 94.6% of 1 GiB, 1 TiB, 20 TiB
steps.line: Metadata falls from 5.0% to 1.7% to 0.40% of the disk as disks grow.
steps.caption: Metadata shrinks as a share of the disk, from 5.0% to 1.7% to 0.40%, because the journal stops at 1 GiB and larger disks get fewer inodes per byte. A 5% reserve grows with the disk: at 20 TiB it is 1 TiB, 12.4 times the metadata.
steps.picture: “mkfs.ext4 -m 5, shares of each disk”, 3 labelled values. This case: 1 GiB: metadata 5.0%, root reserve 5.0%, users 88.5%.

steps.title: A new 20 TiB disk: users can write only 94.6% of it
steps.line: Predict: no file is written yet. Where did 1106.5 GiB go?
steps.caption: We ran mkfs.ext4 1.47.3 with no options on an empty 20 TiB disk, 5,368,709,120 blocks of 4096 bytes, mounted it and asked the kernel’s statfs, which df reads. A user other than root can write 5,078,643,681 blocks, which df shows as Avail: 94.6% of the disk. The other 290,065,439 blocks, 5.4%, are unavailable to this writer before any user files are added. Does unavailable mean already occupied? Predict where they went.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 20 TiB”: 2 slices; “statfs after mkfs.ext4”, 4 labelled values.

steps.title: Answer: 5% is held back for root, 12.4 times all the metadata
steps.line: Predict: what fills the 21,625,887 blocks of metadata?
steps.caption: On a disk of 1 GiB or more, the default 5% reserve for root takes as much space as all the metadata, or more. Without -m, mke2fs reserves 5% of the blocks for root, 268,435,456 here, held back for privileged use. Those blocks can still be free: the reserve changes who may fill them, not whether metadata occupies them. The metadata, the filesystem’s own structures, is 21,625,887 blocks, 0.40%, and once mounted the kernel holds back 4,096 more, 0.000076%, too thin to draw. Free blocks less both reserves is what ordinary users can write. Lowering the root reserve can change that availability without removing a single metadata block.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 20 TiB”: 3 slices; “Where the blocks go”, 7 labelled values. The answer: Root reserve: 5.0%. New in this step: Metadata: 0.4%; “Where the blocks go”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: Inode tables are 97.0% of the metadata
steps.line: One 256-byte inode per 64 KiB of disk: 335,544,320 inodes.
steps.caption: This pie’s whole is the 21,625,887 metadata blocks. An inode records one file, so mke2fs sets aside a fixed number up front, by the disk’s size type: one inode per 16 KiB of disk for the default type, 512 MiB to under 4 TiB; per 32 KiB for big, under 16 TiB; and per 64 KiB for huge, above that. 20 TiB, of the huge type, gets 335,544,320 inodes of 256 bytes, in tables set aside now: 20,971,520 blocks, 0.39% of the disk.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 21,625,887 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Inode tables”, 6 labelled values. This step: Inode tables: 97.0%.
